title: Participles
intro:
Latin has four participles. They are verbal adjectives: they agree with a noun in gender, number and case, and their tense is relative to the main verb.
  • Present active (loving, at the same time as the main verb): incomplete stem + -ns, -ntis, declined like a 3rd-declension adjective: amāns, amantis; vidēns; mittēns; capiēns; audiēns.
  • Perfect passive (having been loved, before the main verb): the 4th principal part, declined like clārus: amātus, -a, -um; vīsus; missus; captus; audītus.
  • Future active (about to love, after the main verb): 4th principal part stem + -ūrus, -a, -um: amātūrus; vīsūrus; missūrus; captūrus; audītūrus.
  • Future passive / gerundive (to be loved, needing to be loved): incomplete stem + -ndus, -a, -um: amandus; videndus; mittendus; capiendus; audiendus.

Watch out: the present participle has a long vowel only in the nominative (amāns, but amantis), and its ablative singular is -e (amante), or often -ī when it is used as a plain adjective. Its neuter plural is -ia (amantia) and its genitive plural -ium.
